summary: A social bee living in colonies of tens of thousands, run by a single egg-laying queen and sterile worker daughters. Its foragers tell nestmates where food lies through a coded dance, and its stored nectar became honey, one of humanity's oldest sweeteners.
nativeRange: Africa, Europe and Western Asia; introduced worldwide by beekeepers
abilities: Waggle dance encodes the direction and distance of food relative to the sun
Workers fan wings and evaporate water to turn nectar into honey of about 18% moisture
Colonies hold brood near 35 °C by shivering flight muscles in winter and evaporative cooling in summer
Swarms choose a new home through a quorum-based scout 'debate'
Can perceive polarised and ultraviolet light to navigate under cloud
Produces honey, beeswax, propolis and royal jelly

uses.use: Medical-grade honey (e.g. Leptospermum/manuka honey dressings) used on burns and wounds
Honey listed as a wound salve in the Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri
Honey described as 'healing for people' in the Qur'an (Surah An-Nahl 16:69)
Propolis as an antiseptic resin; bee venom therapy for joint pain

medicinal.cautions: Never give honey to infants under 12 months (infant botulism). Stings and bee products can cause severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis; bee venom therapy has caused deaths.

animal.diet: Nectar and pollen; larvae fed brood food and royal jelly
animal.habitat: Tree cavities, rock crevices and managed hives near flowering vegetation
animal.lifespan: Workers 5–7 weeks in summer, up to 5 months in winter; queens 2–5 years
animal.behaviour: A forager returning from a rich patch performs a figure-eight dance on the vertical comb; the angle of its waggle run from vertical equals the angle of the food from the sun.
fieldMarks: Slim, hairy worker about 12–15 mm, amber-brown to dark with paler abdominal bands
Two pairs of wings; hind legs carry flattened pollen baskets, often loaded with coloured pollen
Elbowed antennae; flies straight between flowers and hive
Workers from one colony visit one flower type per trip
animal.voice: A steady hum from the wingbeats; a disturbed colony rises to a higher, sharper buzz
animal.lookalikes: Hoverflies mimic bees but have only one pair of wings, very short antennae, large eyes and hover in place. Wasps (Vespula) are glossy, nearly hairless and bright yellow-and-black. Bumblebees are larger, rounder and much furrier.
animal.whereToSee: Flowering orchards, gardens and meadows almost anywhere people keep bees; colonies also nest wild in tree hollows
animal.season: Temperate regions: foraging from early spring to autumn on warm days, clustered in the hive over winter; active all year in the tropics

lore: Honey hunting is painted on Mesolithic rock at the Cuevas de la Araña in Spain (~8,000 years ago), and Egyptian pharaohs used the bee as the hieroglyph for Lower Egypt. Karl von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for decoding its dance.
funFact: To make one kilogram of honey, foragers collectively fly roughly the distance of several trips around the Earth and visit millions of flowers.

summary: An orange-and-black butterfly whose eastern North American population flies up to about 4,800 km to winter in a few mountain fir forests in central Mexico. No individual makes the round trip: the journey north is completed over several generations by its descendants.
nativeRange: North, Central and South America; established in Australia, New Zealand, Pacific islands, Iberia and the Canaries
abilities: Navigates with a time-compensated sun compass housed in its antennae and brain
Can sense Earth's magnetic field as a backup compass
Caterpillars sequester toxic cardenolides from milkweed, making adults distasteful to birds
The autumn 'super generation' lives up to ~8 months, versus 2–6 weeks for summer generations
Clusters by the millions on single trees in Mexico's oyamel forests

animal.diet: Larvae eat milkweeds (Asclepias); adults drink nectar
animal.habitat: Open fields and meadows with milkweed; overwinters in high-altitude fir forest or coastal Californian groves
animal.lifespan: 2–6 weeks for summer adults; up to 8 months for migrants
animal.behaviour: Migrants enter reproductive diapause, travel south on thermals and tailwinds, and roost in dense clusters that keep them cool but above freezing all winter.
fieldMarks: Large orange butterfly with heavy black veins
Black wing borders with two rows of white spots
Males have a small black scent spot on a vein of each hindwing
Caterpillar banded yellow, black and white, on milkweed
animal.lookalikes: Viceroy (Limenitis archippus) is smaller and has a black line crossing the hindwing veins. Queen (Danaus gilippus) is darker chestnut with white spots scattered on the forewing and much thinner black veins.
animal.whereToSee: Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve in Michoacán, Mexico (El Rosario, Sierra Chincua); Pacific Grove and Pismo Beach groves in California; Point Pelee and Cape May during the autumn migration
animal.season: Mexico roosts Nov–Mar; California groves Nov–Feb; breeding across the US and Canada in summer; southward migration Aug–Oct

lore: The Purépecha and Mazahua people of Michoacán long linked the butterflies' arrival in early November with the Day of the Dead and the returning souls of ancestors. Scientists only located the Mexican wintering grounds in 1975, with help from local residents.
funFact: The migratory North American subspecies was listed as Endangered by the IUCN in 2022, then reassessed as Vulnerable in 2023; the species as a whole is Least Concern.

summary: A large, furry social bee that can fly in cold weather and is reared commercially to pollinate greenhouse tomatoes. It buzzes flowers at a precise frequency to shake out pollen honey bees cannot reach.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western Asia; introduced to Chile, Argentina, Tasmania, New Zealand and Japan
abilities: Sonication ('buzz pollination'): vibrates flight muscles to shake pollen from tomato and blueberry flowers
Warms its thorax above 30 °C by shivering, allowing flight near freezing
Detects the weak electric field of flowers to tell recently visited blooms
Learned to pull strings and roll balls for rewards in laboratory experiments
Leaves scent marks so nestmates skip emptied flowers

animal.diet: Nectar and pollen from a wide range of flowers
animal.habitat: Grassland, heath, gardens and farmland; nests underground in old rodent burrows
animal.lifespan: Workers a few weeks; queens about a year, including hibernation
animal.behaviour: Queens emerge from hibernation in early spring and found a colony alone, incubating their first brood on a wax pot like a bird on eggs.
fieldMarks: Large, furry bumblebee, black with two dark-yellow bands (one on the collar, one on the abdomen)
Queens have a buff to off-white tail
Workers have a white tail, often with a faint buff line where it meets the black
Collar band is darker, more orange-tinged yellow than in similar species
animal.voice: A deep, loud buzz; buzz-pollinates some flowers (e.g. tomatoes) with a higher-pitched vibration
animal.lookalikes: White-tailed bumblebee (Bombus lucorum) has a cleaner, lemon-yellow collar and bright white tail; workers of the two are hard to separate reliably in the field. Garden bumblebee (B. hortorum) has an extra yellow band at the rear of the thorax and a very long face.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, parks and farmland across Europe; common on lavender, comfrey and winter-flowering shrubs
animal.season: Queens emerge Feb–Mar; colonies peak in summer; in southern Britain some colonies stay active through winter on garden flowers

lore: Since the late 1980s Belgian and Dutch breeders have shipped colonies worldwide for greenhouse pollination, replacing hand-vibration of tomato flowers. Its introductions to South America have harmed the native giant bumblebee Bombus dahlbomii.
funFact: The old myth that 'science says bumblebees can't fly' came from applying fixed-wing aerodynamics; their flapping wings generate lift from unsteady vortices.

summary: One of the largest moths on Earth, with a wing area of up to about 400 cm². The adult has no working mouth and lives only on fat stored as a caterpillar, dying within one to two weeks.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia, from India to southern China and Indonesia
abilities: Forewing tips resemble a cobra's head, possibly deterring predators when the moth drops and flaps
Males detect female pheromone with large feathery antennae from far away
Adults survive entirely on larval fat reserves, with vestigial mouthparts
Caterpillars spray a pungent defensive fluid
Cocoons are spun from a coarse brown silk

animal.diet: Larvae eat leaves of citrus, cinnamon, guava, soursop and other trees; adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Lowland tropical and secondary forests
animal.size: Wingspan up to ~25 cm; females larger
animal.behaviour: When disturbed, the moth falls to the ground and slowly flaps, displaying its snake-head wingtips.
fieldMarks: Huge moth with reddish-brown wings banded in white, pink and purple
A triangular, scale-less translucent 'window' in each wing
Forewing tips hooked and patterned like a snake's head
Males have broad feathery antennae; females are larger with thinner antennae
animal.lookalikes: Attacus taprobanis of southern India and Sri Lanka is very similar and was once treated as a subspecies; other Attacus species are also called 'Atlas moths'. The New World Rothschildia moths look alike but live only in the Americas.
animal.season: Adults can appear all year but are most numerous Nov–Jan; each adult lives only one to two weeks

lore: In Taiwan the empty cocoons have been used as small purses, and its coarse silk has been spun experimentally. Its name may refer to the Titan Atlas or to the map-like patterns on its wings.
funFact: Its Cantonese name means 'snake's head moth', after the wingtip pattern.

summary: North America's most familiar firefly, a beetle that courts with flashes of cold yellow-green light. Males trace a J-shaped 'swoop' as they flash, and females answer from the grass.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America, south to northern South America
abilities: Produces light through the luciferin–luciferase reaction with very little heat
Males flash a species-specific timed pattern; females reply after a set delay
Larvae glow too and hunt snails, slugs and worms
Contains defensive lucibufagins that make it distasteful to predators

animal.diet: Larvae eat soft-bodied invertebrates; adults eat little or nothing
animal.habitat: Open fields, lawns, forest edges and moist ground
animal.lifespan: About 1–2 years, mostly as a larva; adults a few weeks
animal.behaviour: At dusk a male rises while flashing, drawing a J in the air; a receptive female answers with a single flash after about two seconds.
fieldMarks: Flat, soft-bodied beetle 1–1.4 cm long, dark wing covers edged yellow
Head shield (pronotum) yellow with a black central spot ringed pink or red
Males have lanterns on the last three abdominal segments; females a small lantern on one segment
Males fly low in a J-shaped swoop, flashing on the upswing
animal.voice: Silent; signals with light. The male's yellow flash comes every 5–7 seconds and the female answers from the grass 1–2 seconds later
animal.lookalikes: Photuris fireflies are longer and leggier, flash later into the night with different patterns, and females mimic Photinus replies to eat the males. Many other Photinus species differ chiefly in flash rhythm.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, meadows and woodland edges across the eastern and central United States, including suburban yards
animal.season: Late spring and summer (mainly Jun–Jul), flashing from dusk for about an hour

lore: The firefly luciferase gene, cloned from this species in 1985, became a standard tool in molecular biology for reporting gene activity and detecting ATP. Predatory Photuris 'femme fatale' fireflies mimic its female's reply to lure and eat males.
funFact: Its light reaction gives off almost no heat, and about 40% of reactions produce a photon (Ando et al. 2008) — far lower than the once-quoted ~90%, but still among the most efficient light-producing reactions in nature.

summary: A nocturnal African dung beetle that shapes dung into a ball and rolls it away in a straight line. It is the first animal known to orient by the band of the Milky Way.
nativeRange: Southern Africa
abilities: Holds a straight course using the light gradient of the Milky Way on moonless nights
Climbs onto its ball and 'dances' to take a celestial snapshot before rolling
Buries dung, recycling nutrients and aerating soil
Reduces fly breeding and parasite loads in grazing land

animal.diet: Dung of herbivores
animal.habitat: Open savanna and grassland with large grazing mammals
animal.behaviour: Each beetle races away from the competitive dung pile in a straight line, the quickest way to escape ball thieves.
fieldMarks: Matte black beetle about 2–3 cm long
Broad, shovel-like head edged with teeth
Front legs flattened and toothed for digging and shaping dung
Rolls a dung ball backwards with its hind legs
animal.lookalikes: Southern Africa has many similar ball-rolling Scarabaeus species; telling them apart needs close examination of the head, legs and body sculpture.
animal.season: Active in the southern summer and rainy season, when fresh dung is plentiful

lore: Ancient Egyptians saw the ball-rolling scarab as Khepri pushing the sun across the sky, and carved scarab amulets by the thousands. In 2013 Marie Dacke and colleagues showed this species navigates by the Milky Way, testing it in the Johannesburg planetarium.
funFact: Researchers fitted beetles with tiny cardboard caps to block their view of the sky; capped beetles wandered in circles.

summary: A neotropical ant that cuts fresh leaves not to eat but to feed an underground fungus garden it farms. A mature colony can hold millions of workers, among the most complex animal societies outside humans.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to northern South America and Trinidad
abilities: Cultivates the fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus, part of an ant agriculture tens of millions of years old
Secretes antimicrobial compounds and weeds out parasitic fungi such as Escovopsis to protect its gardens
Workers come in sizes from tiny gardeners to large soldiers, each with its own task
Moves enormous volumes of soil, building nests several metres deep
Clears trails across the forest floor for thousands of foragers

animal.diet: Fungus grown on cut leaves and flowers
animal.habitat: Tropical forest and clearings; nests underground
animal.behaviour: Tiny 'minim' workers often ride on cut leaves, guarding carriers from parasitic flies that try to lay eggs on them.
fieldMarks: Reddish-brown spiny ants in long, cleared trails, carrying leaf pieces held above their heads
Workers in a single column range from tiny to large, big-headed soldiers
Three pairs of spines on the thorax
Huge nest mounds of bare, excavated soil with many entrances
animal.lookalikes: Acromyrmex leafcutters also carry leaves but have four pairs of spines on the thorax and lack Atta's giant-headed soldiers. Soldiers bite hard; watch trails without handling the ants.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforests and clearings of Central America, e.g. La Selva and Corcovado in Costa Rica, Tikal in Guatemala and Barro Colorado Island in Panama
animal.season: Resident; trails busiest at night and in the early morning; winged queens fly at the start of the rainy season

lore: Leafcutters are a long-standing farm pest in Latin America, and their winged queens are roasted and eaten in Colombia as 'hormigas culonas'. Darwin's contemporaries were amazed by their trails, and Thomas Belt in 1874 first argued they farmed fungus.
funFact: Neither ant nor fungus can live without the other: the fungus no longer grows in the wild apart from its farmers.

summary: A southern African termite whose colonies raise mounds several metres high above an underground nest. The mound acts like a lung, exchanging gases with the outside air while the colony farms fungus inside.
nativeRange: Southern and East Africa, including Namibia, Botswana and Kenya
abilities: Builds tall mounds with tunnel networks that use daily temperature swings to drive airflow
Farms Termitomyces fungus to digest wood and grass
Creates nutrient-rich islands that support distinct plants and animals
Workers sense and repair breaches in the mound wall within hours

animal.diet: Dead grass, wood and leaf litter, digested via fungus gardens
animal.habitat: Savanna and dry grassland
animal.size: Workers ~5 mm; queen several cm when swollen
animal.behaviour: The queen can lay many thousands of eggs a day, attended by workers in a sealed royal chamber.
fieldMarks: Tall earthen mounds with a central chimney, often several metres high
Small pale workers and larger soldiers with dark heads and strong jaws
Mounds built of reddish or pale soil matching the local ground
animal.whereToSee: Savanna of northern and central Namibia, where the mounds have been studied near Otjiwarongo
animal.season: Mounds visible all year; winged reproductives swarm after the first heavy summer rains

lore: J. Scott Turner's studies of this species' mounds in Namibia reshaped ideas of how termite mounds ventilate, and inspired 'biomimetic' building designs. Termitomyces mushrooms that sprout from mounds are a prized food across Africa.
funFact: The mound itself is not where termites live; it is an air-conditioning structure over the nest below.

summary: A large dragonfly of North America whose populations make a multigenerational migration, revealed in 2018 by chemical markers in its wings. Adults hunt other insects in the air with very high success.
nativeRange: North America from Canada to Central America and the Caribbean; also Hawaii and parts of East Asia
abilities: Migrates south each autumn and north each spring over three generations
Captures flying prey with a high success rate, intercepting rather than chasing
Has nearly 360° vision from compound eyes
Aquatic nymphs hunt with a hinged, extendable lower lip

animal.diet: Flying insects; nymphs eat aquatic insects, tadpoles and small fish
animal.habitat: Ponds, lakes and slow streams
animal.lifespan: Up to about a year, mostly as a nymph
animal.size: Length ~7–8 cm; wingspan up to 10 cm
animal.behaviour: Pairs often fly in tandem while the female lays eggs into plant stems underwater.
fieldMarks: Large darner with a bright green thorax
Males have a blue abdomen; females and young males greenish to purplish-brown
A dark 'bullseye' spot on top of the face in front of the eyes
Patrols ponds on long, steady beats
animal.lookalikes: Comet darner (Anax longipes) has a bright red abdomen in males and no bullseye. Giant darner (A. walsinghami) is larger and longer-bodied. Other darners (Aeshna) have striped thoraxes.
animal.whereToSee: Ponds and lakes across North America; spectacular autumn migration along coasts, e.g. Cape May Point, New Jersey
animal.season: Resident broods breed in summer; migrants arrive in the north in spring and fly south Aug–Oct

lore: It is the state insect of Washington. Hydrogen isotopes in its wings, studied in 2018, revealed a three-generation annual cycle from Canada to Mexico and back.
funFact: Some were fitted with tiny radio transmitters and followed by small aircraft as they migrated.

summary: The classic red ladybird with seven black spots, a voracious predator of aphids. Gardeners welcome it as one of the oldest natural pest controls.
nativeRange: Europe, Asia and North Africa; introduced to North America
abilities: A single larva can eat hundreds of aphids before pupating
Reflex-bleeds bitter, alkaloid-laden yellow fluid from its leg joints when attacked
Bright warning colours advertise its bad taste
Overwinters in large aggregations

animal.diet: Aphids and other soft-bodied insects; some pollen
animal.habitat: Grassland, crops, gardens and hedgerows
animal.behaviour: Adults cluster in leaf litter or tussocks to hibernate through winter.
fieldMarks: Red domed wing cases with seven black spots (three on each side and one shared at the front)
Black head shield with a whitish patch in each front corner
Black legs
About 7–8 mm long
animal.lookalikes: Harlequin ladybird (Harmonia axyridis) is larger and very variable, often with an M- or W-shaped mark on a white head shield and brown or orange legs. Two-spot ladybird is smaller with only two spots.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, grassland, crops and hedgerows wherever aphids are plentiful
animal.season: Active Mar–Oct; overwinters as an adult in leaf litter and dense vegetation

lore: Its English and German names honour the Virgin Mary ('Our Lady's bird', Marienkäfer), whose red cloak and seven sorrows the colours and spots were said to recall. It was released in the USA repeatedly to control aphids, and wild populations were established there by the 1970s.
funFact: Its seven spots are fixed for life; they do not indicate age, despite the folk belief.

summary: A moth so thoroughly domesticated over about 5,000 years that it can no longer survive in the wild: adults cannot fly and caterpillars barely search for food. Each cocoon is spun from a single continuous silk thread up to about 900 m long.
nativeRange: Domesticated in China from the wild Bombyx mandarina; now reared in sericulture worldwide
abilities: Spins a cocoon from a single filament of fibroin bound by sericin, up to ~900 m long
Silk is among the strongest natural fibres for its weight
Adults are flightless and do not feed
Male detects the pheromone bombykol, the first insect pheromone ever identified (1959)
Genome engineered to produce spider-silk and medical proteins

uses.use: Braided silk sutures, used for centuries and still common in surgery
Jiāngcán (僵蚕), larvae killed by the fungus Beauveria bassiana, used for convulsions and sore throat
Silk fibroin scaffolds for tissue engineering and drug delivery

medicinal.cautions: Strong evidence applies to silk sutures as a surgical material only; traditional jiangcan use has little clinical evidence. Silkworm pupae and sericin can cause allergies.

animal.diet: Larvae eat mulberry leaves (Morus); adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Exists only in human care
animal.lifespan: About 6–8 weeks, including ~4 weeks as a caterpillar
animal.size: Caterpillar to ~7.5 cm; adult wingspan ~4–5 cm
animal.behaviour: A caterpillar spins its cocoon in a figure-eight motion for two to three days, swinging its head hundreds of thousands of times.
fieldMarks: Creamy-white, furry moth with stubby wings, unable to fly
Feathery antennae
Pale caterpillar with a small horn at the tail, feeding on mulberry leaves
Spins a cocoon of a single continuous silk thread
animal.lookalikes: Its wild ancestor Bombyx mandarina is brown and can fly; the domestic silkmoth exists only in captivity.

lore: Chinese legend credits Leizu, wife of the Yellow Emperor, with discovering silk when a cocoon fell into her tea. China guarded the secret for centuries until, by Procopius's account, monks smuggled eggs to Byzantium in hollow canes around 552 CE.
funFact: The Silk Road takes its name from this insect's thread, coined by Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.

summary: A large rainforest butterfly whose electric blue contains no blue pigment at all. The colour comes from nanoscale ridges on its wing scales that interfere with light.
nativeRange: Central America and northern South America, including the Amazon basin
abilities: Structural colour: Christmas-tree-shaped nanostructures reflect blue light through interference
The underside is brown with eyespots, so it flashes and vanishes as it flaps
Scales repel water and are studied for anti-counterfeiting inks and sensors
Adults ferment-feed on rotting fruit

animal.diet: Larvae eat legumes; adults drink juices of rotting fruit, sap and fungi
animal.habitat: Tropical rainforest, especially along streams and clearings
animal.behaviour: Males patrol sunlit river corridors, their flashing wings visible from far away, even from low-flying aircraft.
fieldMarks: Very large butterfly, upperside brilliant iridescent blue edged with black
Underside brown with rows of eyespots, giving a blue flicker in flight
Females duller above
Rises and dips in a slow, flapping flight along streams
animal.season: Seen all year in the tropics; mostly active in mid-morning sun

lore: Morpho wings were used in 19th- and early-20th-century European jewellery and trays. The genus name recalls Morpho, an epithet of Aphrodite.
funFact: Drop alcohol on a morpho wing and it turns green until the liquid evaporates, because the gaps in the nanostructure fill with a different medium.

summary: A pink-and-white mantis with petal-shaped legs that looks like a flower. It does not hide on orchids but sits in the open and lures pollinating insects to itself.
nativeRange: Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and nearby Southeast Asia
abilities: Aggressive mimicry of a generic flower that attracts pollinators
Lured more pollinators than real flowers in field experiments (O'Hanlon et al. 2014)
To bee and fly eyes its colour is hard to distinguish from real flowers
Can shift colour slightly between pink and white

animal.diet: Bees, flies, butterflies and other flower-visiting insects
animal.habitat: Shrubs and flowers in rainforest
animal.behaviour: Females are more than twice the size of males; tiny males avoid being eaten by approaching cautiously.
fieldMarks: White to pink mantis shaped like an orchid petal
Walking legs with broad, petal-like lobes
Females much larger than males
Sits motionless on or near flowers

lore: An 1879 account by the traveller James Hingston described a mantis from Java catching butterflies while posing as an orchid, fuelling Victorian fascination with mimicry.
funFact: Young nymphs are red and black, mimicking a foul-tasting assassin bug before they turn pink.

summary: A golden dragonfly found on every continent except Antarctica, holding the record for the longest insect migration. Generations cross the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa, riding monsoon winds.
nativeRange: Tropics and warm temperate zones worldwide
abilities: Multigenerational migration estimated at 14,000–18,000 km round trip across the Indian Ocean
Flies for days with little effort, gliding on broad hindwings
Breeds in temporary rain pools, with larvae developing in ~5 weeks
Genetic studies show near-global gene flow between continents

animal.diet: Small flying insects; aquatic larvae eat mosquito larvae and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Open areas near temporary freshwater pools
animal.behaviour: Swarms gather ahead of rain fronts, following winds to new rains where pools will form.
fieldMarks: Golden-yellow to orange skimmer about 4.5 cm long
Wings clear and very broad at the hindwing base
Large reddish eyes take up most of the head
Flies for hours on end, gliding high over open ground
animal.lookalikes: Spot-winged glider (Pantala hymenaea) has an obvious brown spot at the base of each hindwing and is slightly darker; saddlebags (Tramea) have a dark band at the hindwing base.
animal.whereToSee: Open ground and paddy fields across the tropics; notable on the Maldives during its ocean crossing between India and East Africa
animal.season: Follows the rains; in India swarms arrive with the monsoons, and the return from Africa reaches India's west coast from May

lore: Biologist Charles Anderson noticed swarms arriving in the Maldives every October with no fresh water for breeding, and in 2009 proposed the transoceanic migration. In Japan it is associated with the Obon festival as 'spirit dragonfly'.
funFact: It is the highest-flying dragonfly recorded, seen at about 6,200 m in the Himalaya.

summary: A grasshopper that transforms when crowded: it changes colour, behaviour and body shape, and forms swarms that can cover hundreds of square kilometres. A swarm can eat as much in a day as millions of people.
nativeRange: Deserts from West Africa through the Arabian Peninsula to India
abilities: Phase change: crowding triggers serotonin release that switches it from solitary to gregarious form
Swarms travel up to ~150 km a day on winds
Crossed the Atlantic from West Africa to the Caribbean in 1988
A locust eats about its own weight in fresh food daily

animal.diet: Almost any green vegetation, including crops
animal.habitat: Desert and semi-desert, swarming far beyond into farmland
animal.behaviour: Solitary green nymphs avoid each other; once crowded they turn yellow and black, march in bands and seek company.
fieldMarks: Large grasshopper, 6–8 cm, with long wings reaching past the abdomen tip
Solitary phase sandy, grey or greenish
Gregarious phase: immature adults pink, mature males bright yellow; hoppers yellow-and-black
Forewings with large irregular dark spots
animal.season: Breeds after rains; swarms are unpredictable and follow unusual rainfall

lore: The eighth plague of Egypt in Exodus is locusts, and John the Baptist ate 'locusts and wild honey'. Locusts are one of the few insects declared kosher in Leviticus, and are still eaten in parts of Yemen and Morocco.
funFact: Solitary and swarming forms looked so different that they were long classified as separate species, until Boris Uvarov showed in 1921 they were phases of one.

summary: A pink-and-olive hawk-moth that hovers at flowers at dusk. It was the first animal shown to see colour in dim starlight, when humans see only grey.
nativeRange: Europe and temperate Asia to Japan
abilities: Colour vision under starlight using highly sensitive superposition eyes (Kelber et al. 2002)
Hovers while drinking nectar through a long proboscis
Caterpillar inflates its eyespots to mimic a small snake

animal.diet: Larvae eat willowherb (Chamaenerion) and bedstraw (Galium); adults drink nectar from honeysuckle and similar flowers
animal.habitat: Gardens, rough ground, heaths and woodland edges
animal.behaviour: When disturbed, the caterpillar pulls its head in and swells its front segments, flashing four eyespots like a snake.
fieldMarks: Olive-green and pink moth with a streamlined body
Pink bands across the olive forewing and a pink body
Caterpillar grey-brown with two pairs of eyespots behind a trunk-like head
Visits flowers at dusk
animal.lookalikes: Small elephant hawk-moth (Deilephila porcellus) is smaller and mainly pink and yellowish-brown, without the olive-green bands.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens with honeysuckle, rough ground with rosebay willowherb, heaths and woodland edges across Europe
animal.season: Adults May–Jul; caterpillars Jul–Sep on willowherbs, bedstraws and fuchsia

lore: The common name refers to the trunk-like caterpillar. Linnaeus named it after Elpenor, Odysseus's companion who fell from Circe's roof.
funFact: It is a common garden visitor in Britain, yet its night colour vision was only discovered in 2002.

summary: Europe's largest bee, glossy black with violet-tinted wings. Females carve nest tunnels into dead wood with their jaws.
nativeRange: Southern and Central Europe, North Africa, West and Central Asia
abilities: Excavates nest tunnels in dead wood using strong mandibles
Buzz-pollinates some flowers
Robs nectar by slitting holes at the base of long flowers
Adults overwinter and can live about a year

animal.diet: Nectar and pollen from many plants, e.g. wisteria, lavender and legumes
animal.habitat: Warm, open areas with dead wood
animal.behaviour: A solitary female builds a row of cells in her tunnel, each sealed with chewed wood pulp and stocked with pollen.
fieldMarks: Large, stout bee, 2–3 cm, glossy black with a blue-violet sheen
Dark wings with a strong violet iridescence
Loud, heavy flight between flowers
Bores round holes in dead wood
animal.voice: A deep, loud drone
animal.lookalikes: Other European carpenter bees (X. valga, X. iris) look similar and need close study to separate. Bumblebees are furrier with coloured bands.
animal.whereToSee: Warm gardens, vineyards and old wooden structures in southern and central Europe
animal.season: Adults overwinter and emerge in spring (usually Apr–May); new adults appear in late summer

lore: In recent decades it has spread north into Britain and the Netherlands with warming climate.
funFact: Despite its size and loud buzz, it is docile, and males have no sting.

summary: The only hummingbird that breeds widely in eastern North America. Weighing about 3 g, many cross the Gulf of Mexico nonstop, roughly 800 km, each spring and autumn.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern North America; winters in Mexico and Central America
abilities: Flies nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, nearly doubling its weight in fat beforehand
Beats wings around 50–80 times per second and can hover and fly backwards
Enters nightly torpor, dropping body temperature to save energy
Pollinates tubular red flowers such as trumpet creeper and cardinal flower

animal.diet: Nectar, plus small insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Open woodland, forest edges, gardens
animal.behaviour: Males perform U-shaped pendulum display dives in front of perched females.
fieldMarks: Tiny hummingbird with bright emerald back
Male has a glowing ruby-red throat that can look black in poor light
Female has a white throat and white-tipped tail feathers
Forked dark tail in males
animal.voice: Soft, rapid 'chew' chips and squeaky chatter; male wings make a high hum
animal.lookalikes: Black-chinned hummingbird (mainly western) male has a black chin with a narrow violet band; females of the two are very hard to separate. Rufous hummingbird is orange.
animal.whereToSee: Garden feeders across eastern North America; spring migrants on the Texas coast, e.g. High Island
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Sep in the east; winters in Mexico and Central America

lore: To the Aztecs, hummingbirds were linked with Huitzilopochtli, whose name means 'hummingbird of the south', and fallen warriors were thought to return as hummingbirds.
funFact: Its heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute in flight.

summary: A fiery orange hummingbird that makes one of the longest migrations of any bird relative to body size, travelling about 6,000 km between Alaska and Mexico. It is famously aggressive at flowers and feeders.
nativeRange: Breeds from Oregon to southern Alaska; winters mainly in Mexico, increasingly along the US Gulf Coast
abilities: Migrates about 6,000 km one way, roughly 78 million body lengths
Takes a clockwise loop route, north along the Pacific coast and south along the Rockies to follow flowering
Breeds farther north than any other hummingbird
Remembers individual flowers and when it last emptied them

animal.diet: Nectar and small insects
animal.habitat: Open coniferous forest, meadows and gardens
animal.behaviour: Males defend flower patches fiercely, chasing off much larger birds and other hummingbirds.
fieldMarks: Small, bright orange-rufous hummingbird
Male has an iridescent orange-red throat and rufous back
Female green above with rufous flanks and tail base
Aggressive at flowers and feeders
animal.voice: Hard 'chewp' chips; adult male wings make a metallic trill
animal.lookalikes: Allen's hummingbird is nearly identical; males usually have a green back, but some rufous males show green too, so many females and young can only be identified by tail-feather shape in the hand.
animal.whereToSee: Pacific Northwest and Alaskan forests and gardens; mountain meadows of the Rockies on autumn passage
animal.season: Breeds Mar–Aug in the Northwest; moves south through the Rockies Jul–Sep

lore: It was described from Nootka Sound, Vancouver Island, during the voyages of James Cook in 1778.
funFact: Its population has fallen by more than half since 1970, and IUCN moved it to Near Threatened in 2018.

summary: A rose-headed hummingbird of the Pacific coast whose courtship dive is, relative to body length, among the fastest known movements of any vertebrate. At the bottom of the dive its tail feathers sing.
nativeRange: Western North America from British Columbia to Baja California and Arizona
abilities: Display dive reaches ~385 body lengths per second (Clark 2009)
Outer tail feathers flutter to make a loud chirp at the bottom of the dive
Withstands around 9 g of acceleration pulling out of the dive
Stays through winter in the north, aided by garden feeders and exotic plants

animal.diet: Nectar, insects and tree sap from sapsucker wells
animal.habitat: Gardens, parks, chaparral and open woodland
animal.behaviour: A male climbs up to 40 m and plunges in a J-shaped dive past a female, ending in a sharp tail-feather chirp.
fieldMarks: Medium-sized hummingbird, green above, greyish below
Male has an iridescent rose-pink crown and throat
Female often shows a small central patch of pink on the throat
Short straight bill
animal.voice: Male gives a scratchy, buzzy song from a perch; display dive ends in a loud chirp made by the tail feathers
animal.lookalikes: Costa's hummingbird is smaller with a purple crown and a throat patch that flares down the sides. Rufous and Allen's are orange.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, parks and chaparral along the Pacific Coast from Vancouver to Baja California
animal.season: Resident; breeds in winter and spring

lore: It is named after Anna Masséna, Duchess of Rivoli, a 19th-century French collector of hummingbird specimens.
funFact: Its range has expanded northward to Vancouver and beyond since the mid-20th century.

summary: The smallest bird in the world, about 5–6 cm long and under 2 g, found only in Cuba. Its eggs are the size of coffee beans.
nativeRange: Endemic to Cuba and the Isla de la Juventud
abilities: World's smallest bird, weighing about 1.6–2 g
Has one of the highest metabolic rates of any warm-blooded animal
Visits up to 1,500 flowers in a day

animal.diet: Nectar and small insects
animal.habitat: Forest, woodland edges and gardens with flowering plants
animal.behaviour: Females build a cup nest about 2.5 cm across, woven from cobwebs, lichen and bark.
fieldMarks: World's smallest bird, about 5–6 cm
Breeding male has an iridescent fiery red-pink head and throat with long lateral plumes
Upperparts bluish; female green above, pale below with white-tipped tail
Very short tail and tiny body
animal.voice: A high-pitched, jumbled twitter, often sung from a treetop
animal.lookalikes: Cuban emerald is much larger, all green with a forked tail.
animal.whereToSee: Zapata Swamp, Cuba (e.g. around Bermejas and Playa Larga); also Alejandro de Humboldt National Park
animal.season: Resident; breeds mainly Mar–Jun

lore: It was described in the 1840s from Cuba and appears on Cuban postage stamps; Cubans call it zunzuncito after its buzzing.
funFact: It is smaller than some of the moths that share its flowers.

summary: The fastest animal on Earth, reaching more than 320 km/h when stooping on prey. Wiped out from much of its range by DDT in the 1960s, it has recovered and now nests on city skyscrapers.
nativeRange: Every continent except Antarctica
abilities: Stoops at speeds recorded up to about 389 km/h
Bony tubercles in its nostrils deflect air so it can breathe in high-speed dives
Arctic-breeding populations migrate up to ~25,000 km a year
Has a third eyelid to protect its eyes in dives

animal.diet: Mainly birds caught in flight, such as pigeons, ducks and shorebirds
animal.habitat: Cliffs, coasts, open country, and tall buildings in cities
animal.behaviour: It climbs high above prey, folds its wings and drops in a steep stoop, striking with clenched talons.
fieldMarks: Powerful falcon with long pointed wings and a medium tail
Adult blue-grey above with a dark 'helmet' and broad moustache stripe
Pale underparts finely barred
Young birds brown above with streaked underparts
animal.voice: A harsh, rasping 'kak-kak-kak' near the nest
animal.lookalikes: Prairie falcon is pale brown with dark 'armpits'. Lanner falcon has a rufous crown and thinner moustache. Gyrfalcon is bulkier with broader wings. Hobby is smaller with rufous 'trousers'.
animal.whereToSee: Sea cliffs and city buildings; many urban nests carry public webcams (e.g. Derby Cathedral, UK); migrants at Cape May and Falsterbo
animal.season: Resident in much of its range; Arctic breeders migrate long distances

lore: Prized in falconry from Mongolia to the Arab world; the 15th-century Boke of St Albans assigned it to earls. Its crash from DDT-thinned eggshells helped drive the US ban of DDT in 1972.
funFact: Its name means 'wanderer', because falconers caught young birds on migration rather than taking them from nests.

summary: A sea eagle of North America, the national bird of the United States. It builds the largest nests of any North American bird, used and added to for decades.
nativeRange: Most of North America, from Alaska and Canada to northern Mexico
abilities: Builds nests up to ~3 m wide and weighing over a tonne
Snatches fish from the water surface with its talons
Steals prey from ospreys and other birds (kleptoparasitism)
Gathers by the thousands along salmon rivers in winter

animal.diet: Mainly fish; also waterbirds and carrion
animal.habitat: Near large water bodies with tall trees
animal.lifespan: Around 20 years in the wild; record about 38
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform cartwheel courtship flights, locking talons and spinning downward together.
fieldMarks: Adult has a white head and tail and dark brown body
Massive yellow hooked bill
Young birds mottled brown and white for 4–5 years
Flat, plank-like wings when soaring
animal.voice: A weak, high-pitched twittering chatter, surprising for its size
animal.lookalikes: Golden eagle (vs young bald eagle) has a golden nape, smaller head and bill, and legs feathered to the toes; young goldens show neat white wing patches and a white tail base, not blotchy mottling.
animal.whereToSee: Chilkat Bald Eagle Preserve near Haines, Alaska; Conowingo Dam, Maryland; locks and dams along the Mississippi River in winter
animal.season: Resident in many areas; large winter gatherings Nov–Feb at open water and salmon runs

lore: Sacred to many Native American nations, its feathers are central to ceremony and regulated under US law for tribal use. It became the national emblem in 1782, and its recovery from DDT led to removal from the Endangered Species list in 2007.
funFact: 'Bald' comes from an old meaning of 'piebald' or white-headed, not hairless.

summary: The most widespread eagle in the world, ranging across the Northern Hemisphere. Kazakh hunters in Mongolia still fly trained females to catch foxes.
nativeRange: North America, Europe, North Africa and Asia
abilities: Takes prey as large as young deer and foxes
Can dive at around 240 km/h
Eyesight several times sharper than humans'
Territories can span over 100 km²

animal.diet: Hares, rabbits, marmots, ground squirrels, birds; carrion in winter
animal.habitat: Open mountains, steppe and moorland
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform undulating 'sky-dance' flights, rising and plunging over their territory.
fieldMarks: Very large dark brown eagle with a golden-buff nape
Legs feathered to the toes
Juveniles have white patches in the wings and a white tail base with dark tip
Soars with wings in a shallow V
animal.voice: Usually silent; occasional yelping or mewing calls
animal.lookalikes: Young bald eagles have bigger heads and bills, bare lower legs and blotchy white mottling. White-tailed eagle has a huge bill, short wedge-shaped tail and broad 'barn-door' wings.
animal.whereToSee: Scottish Highlands and islands (e.g. Mull, Cairngorms), the Alps, Denali and the mountain West of North America
animal.season: Resident in most of its range; northern birds move south in winter

lore: Kazakh berkutchi have hunted with golden eagles for centuries, celebrated at the annual Golden Eagle Festival in Bayan-Ölgii. It is the national bird of Mexico, Germany, Albania and Kazakhstan.
funFact: Kazakh eagle hunters have used trained golden eagles to take wolves.

summary: The largest penguin, and the only animal that breeds on Antarctic sea ice through the polar winter. Males incubate a single egg on their feet for about two months without eating.
nativeRange: Coast and sea ice of Antarctica
abilities: Dives to over 500 m (record 564 m) and holds its breath over 27 minutes
Males fast for up to ~115 days during courtship and incubation
Huddles of thousands rotate so each bird takes turns in the warm centre
Survives temperatures below −40 °C and winds over 140 km/h

animal.diet: Fish, krill and squid
animal.habitat: Fast sea ice around Antarctica; forages in open water
animal.behaviour: In the dark of winter, males huddle in tight masses, shuffling so that no bird stays on the cold edge for long.
fieldMarks: Largest penguin, up to about 1.2 m tall
Black head and back, white belly
Pale yellow ear patches fading into a whitish upper breast
Pinkish-orange stripe on the lower bill
animal.voice: Loud, trumpeting contact calls; each bird's call is individually recognisable
animal.lookalikes: King penguin is smaller and slimmer with bright orange, comma-shaped ear patches that are enclosed in black.
animal.whereToSee: Snow Hill Island colony in the Weddell Sea (by icebreaker and helicopter) and Atka Bay; rarely reached by tourists
animal.season: Breeds through the Antarctic winter; chicks visible Oct–Dec

lore: In 1911 Edward Wilson, Apsley Cherry-Garrard and Henry Bowers made 'the worst journey in the world' in Antarctic winter to collect emperor eggs at Cape Crozier.
funFact: Satellite images of the brown guano stains on ice have revealed previously unknown colonies.

summary: A flightless, nocturnal bird of New Zealand that hunts with nostrils at the tip of its long bill. Females lay an egg about a fifth of their own body weight, one of the largest relative to body size of any bird.
nativeRange: North Island of New Zealand
abilities: Only bird with nostrils at the tip of its bill, smelling prey underground
Bill-tip sensory pits detect vibrations of invertebrates
Egg weighs about 15–20% of the mother's weight
Has a body temperature lower than most birds, around 38 °C
Hair-like feathers and tiny vestigial wings

animal.diet: Earthworms, beetle larvae, cicadas, spiders and fallen fruit
animal.habitat: Native and exotic forest, scrub and farmland edges
animal.behaviour: Pairs defend territories with shrill calls at night, and the male incubates the egg for about three months.
fieldMarks: Pear-shaped, flightless bird with no visible wings or tail
Shaggy, streaky reddish-brown feathers
Long, pale, slightly curved bill with nostrils at the tip
Nocturnal, probing the ground
animal.voice: Male gives a shrill, rising whistle repeated many times; female a lower, hoarse cry
animal.lookalikes: It is the only wild kiwi over most of the North Island; little spotted kiwi (on a few island and fenced sanctuaries) is smaller and pale grey with fine mottling.
animal.whereToSee: Trounson Kauri Park night walks (Northland); nocturnal kiwi houses such as Otorohanga Kiwi House
animal.season: Resident

lore: Kiwi are a taonga (treasure) to Māori, and cloaks of kiwi feathers (kahu kiwi) were worn by high-ranking people. The bird gave New Zealanders their nickname.
funFact: Without predator control, around 95% of kiwi chicks die before breeding age, mostly to stoats and cats.

summary: The largest living bird, up to about 2.7 m tall, and the fastest runner on two legs. It lays the largest eggs of any living bird.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa; formerly North Africa and the Middle East
abilities: Runs at about 70 km/h, with strides up to 5 m
Lays eggs about 15 cm long and 1.4 kg
Has the largest eyes of any land vertebrate, around 5 cm across
Has only two toes, an adaptation for running
A forward kick can kill a lion

animal.diet: Plants, seeds and roots; also insects and small animals
animal.habitat: Open savanna, semi-desert and grassland
animal.behaviour: Several females lay in one shared nest; the dominant female and the male take turns incubating, he at night, she by day.
fieldMarks: Tallest bird, flightless, with long bare neck and legs
Males black with white wings and tail; females greyish-brown
Male's neck and legs pinkish, turning red on the shins when breeding
Two toes on each foot
animal.voice: Breeding males give a deep, booming roar
animal.lookalikes: Somali ostrich (a separate species in the Horn of Africa) has blue-grey neck and thigh skin. Ostriches kick hard; watch from a vehicle or at a distance.
animal.whereToSee: Etosha (Namibia), Maasai Mara and Serengeti, and the Cape of Good Hope section of Table Mountain National Park
animal.season: Resident

lore: Ostrich eggshells were engraved by people at Diepkloof Rock Shelter in South Africa about 60,000 years ago, and used as water flasks and beads by San peoples. Ostrich plumes were a fashion craze in Edwardian Europe.
funFact: The story that ostriches bury their heads in sand is a myth, perhaps from seeing them turn eggs in ground nests.

summary: The bird with the longest wingspan alive, up to about 3.5 m. It can circle the Southern Ocean and travel thousands of kilometres with barely a wingbeat.
nativeRange: Southern Ocean; breeds on South Georgia, Crozet, Kerguelen, Prince Edward and Macquarie islands
abilities: Wingspan up to ~3.5 m, the largest of any living bird
Dynamic soaring: harvests energy from wind gradients over waves
A shoulder lock holds wings outstretched with little muscle effort
Can cover over 10,000 km in a single foraging trip
Smells prey and oily slicks from far away with tube nostrils

animal.diet: Squid, fish and carrion taken at the surface
animal.habitat: Open ocean; nests on grassy subantarctic islands
animal.behaviour: Pairs bond for life after years of elaborate dancing with wing-spreading and bill-clapping, and raise one chick every two years.
fieldMarks: Enormous wingspan, often 2.5–3.5 m
Adult males the whitest of the great albatrosses, with black only at the wingtips and trailing edge
Large pink bill
Juveniles chocolate brown with a white face, whitening over many years
animal.voice: At the nest: braying, screams, whistles and loud bill-clapping during courtship dances
animal.lookalikes: Royal albatrosses have a black cutting edge to the upper bill; on adult royals the upperwing whitens from the leading edge back, not from the centre. Several other 'wandering-type' albatrosses (Tristan, Antipodean, Amsterdam) are browner.
animal.whereToSee: Prion Island, South Georgia (boardwalk, cruise landings); at sea in the Drake Passage and Southern Ocean
animal.season: Lays Dec–early Jan; chicks remain at the nest through the austral winter. Prion Island is closed 20 Nov–7 Jan

lore: In Coleridge's 'Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), killing an albatross brings a curse on a ship. Sailors long believed albatrosses carried the souls of drowned seamen.
funFact: Tens of thousands of albatrosses have drowned on longline fishing hooks, the main threat to the species.

summary: The bird with the longest known migration, flying from Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back each year. It probably sees more daylight than any other animal.
nativeRange: Breeds around the Arctic and subarctic; winters in Antarctic waters
abilities: Round-trip migration averaging ~70,000 km a year, up to ~96,000 km
Lifetime travel can equal roughly three trips to the Moon and back
Takes S-shaped routes to ride prevailing winds across oceans
Plunge-dives to catch small fish
Fiercely mobs intruders, including humans, at nests

animal.diet: Small fish and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Coastal tundra, islands and open ocean
animal.behaviour: Experiences two summers each year, following the sun from pole to pole.
fieldMarks: Slender grey-and-white tern with a black cap
All-red bill without a dark tip
Very short red legs
Long tail streamers and translucent flight feathers when seen from below
animal.voice: A harsh, high 'kee-arr' and rattling alarm calls; dive-bombs intruders at colonies
animal.lookalikes: Common tern has a black-tipped orange-red bill, longer legs, a darker wedge on the outer wing and shorter tail streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Farne Islands, Northumberland (wear a hat — the birds strike heads), Iceland and Shetland
animal.season: Northern colonies May–Aug; winters in Antarctic waters

lore: Tracking by Carsten Egevang and colleagues in 2010 with geolocators weighing 1.4 g first mapped its full migration. In Iceland and Greenland its eggs were traditionally gathered.
funFact: A tern ringed as a chick in Britain was found in Australia, over 22,000 km away, within months.

summary: A large white owl of the Arctic tundra that hunts by day in the continuous light of polar summer. Its numbers and breeding rise and fall with lemming cycles.
nativeRange: Circumpolar Arctic; winters south into Canada, the northern USA, Europe and Asia
abilities: Hunts in 24-hour daylight, unlike most owls
Thick feathering, including on the toes, insulates against −50 °C
Nomadic: travels widely to breed where lemmings are abundant
Clutch size varies from 0 to over 10 eggs depending on prey
Periodically 'irrupts' far south in winter

animal.diet: Lemmings and voles; also hares, birds and fish
animal.habitat: Open tundra; winters on prairies, coasts and airfields
animal.behaviour: An adult can eat over 1,600 lemmings a year.
fieldMarks: Large white owl with yellow eyes
Adult males nearly pure white
Females and young heavily barred with black
Round head with no visible ear tufts
animal.voice: Males give a deep, booming hoot on the breeding grounds; usually silent in winter
animal.lookalikes: Barn owl is smaller, with a heart-shaped face, dark eyes and golden-buff upperparts.
animal.whereToSee: Boundary Bay, British Columbia and Amherst Island, Ontario in winter; tundra near Utqiaġvik, Alaska in summer
animal.season: Tundra breeder; winter visitor further south Nov–Mar, with large irruptions in some years

lore: Its image appears in Paleolithic art at the Trois-Frères cave in France, and it is the official bird of Quebec. Hedwig in the Harry Potter stories made it world-famous.
funFact: Adult males grow whiter with age, and some old males are almost pure white.

summary: The world's only flightless parrot and the heaviest parrot, a nocturnal, moss-green bird from New Zealand. Every surviving individual has a name and is closely monitored.
nativeRange: New Zealand; now survives only on predator-free islands such as Whenua Hou and Anchor Island
abilities: Heaviest parrot, up to ~4 kg
Males 'boom' with a call that can carry several kilometres
Breeds only in years when rimu trees fruit heavily
Can live 60–90 years, among the longest-lived birds
Climbs trees and parachutes down on short wings

animal.diet: Leaves, shoots, seeds, fruit and pollen; rimu fruit in breeding years
animal.habitat: Native forest and scrub on predator-free islands
animal.behaviour: Males gather at leks and dig bowl-shaped hollows from which they boom nightly for months to attract females.
fieldMarks: Large, flightless, moss-green parrot finely barred with black and yellow
Owl-like facial disc of whiskery feathers
Heavy grey bill
Nocturnal; climbs trees and walks
animal.voice: Males 'boom' with a deep, resonant sound that carries kilometres, followed by a metallic 'ching'
animal.lookalikes: Kea and kākā are flying parrots; kea is olive-green with orange underwings and lives in the mountains.
animal.whereToSee: Its predator-free breeding islands are closed to the public
animal.season: Breeds only in years when rimu trees fruit heavily; males boom in summer (about Dec–Mar) of those years

lore: Māori hunted kākāpō for food and made feather cloaks (kahu kākāpō). By 1995 only 51 birds remained; a national recovery programme has since more than quadrupled the population.
funFact: A male named Sirocco became famous for trying to mate with a zoologist's head on television in 2009.

summary: A pheasant-sized songbird of south-eastern Australia and one of the greatest vocal mimics on Earth. Males copy the calls of dozens of other species, and occasionally human-made sounds.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia; introduced to Tasmania
abilities: Mimics the calls of many other birds with near-perfect accuracy
Has been recorded imitating camera shutters, chainsaws and car alarms
Males choreograph songs to specific dance movements
Rakes enormous volumes of forest litter, an important ecosystem engineer

animal.diet: Earthworms, insects, spiders and other invertebrates from the forest floor
animal.habitat: Wet forests and gullies
animal.size: Males up to ~1 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Males sing on cleared mounds, spreading the lyre-shaped tail over their heads in a shimmering display.
fieldMarks: Pheasant-sized brown ground bird
Males have a long tail of 16 feathers, including two lyre-shaped outer feathers
Females have a long, plainer tail
Strong legs; scratches leaf litter
animal.voice: Loud, powerful song full of near-perfect imitations of other birds and sometimes mechanical sounds, mixed with its own ringing calls
animal.lookalikes: Albert's lyrebird of the NSW–Queensland border rainforests is more rufous and males lack the lyre-shaped outer tail feathers.
animal.whereToSee: Sherbrooke Forest (Dandenong Ranges) near Melbourne, the Blue Mountains and Royal National Park near Sydney
animal.season: Resident; most song and display in winter (Jun–Aug)

lore: It appears on the reverse of the Australian 10-cent coin. A lyrebird population in New England National Park is said to sing a flute tune taught to captive birds in the 1930s.
funFact: A single lyrebird can move around 155 tonnes of soil and litter per hectare per year.

summary: An iridescent green trogon of Central American cloud forests whose breeding males grow tail-covert streamers up to about 65 cm long, making the bird about 1 m long. It was sacred to the Maya and Aztecs and is Guatemala's national bird.
nativeRange: Cloud forests from southern Mexico to western Panama
abilities: Males grow streaming tail coverts longer than their body
Swallows wild avocados whole and regurgitates the pits, dispersing laurel tree seeds
Its green is structural colour, shifting from gold to blue
Migrates up and down mountains following fruiting trees

animal.diet: Fruit, especially wild avocados (Lauraceae); also insects and small frogs
animal.habitat: Humid montane cloud forest
animal.size: 36–40 cm, plus male tail streamers up to ~65 cm
animal.behaviour: Pairs nest in holes in rotting trees; the male's tail often pokes out of the entrance while he incubates.
fieldMarks: Male shimmering emerald-green with a crimson belly
Male's long green tail streamers up to about 65 cm
Helmet-like crest and yellow bill
Female duller green with grey breast and no streamers
animal.voice: A repeated, mellow 'kyow' and whistled 'kee-oo'
animal.lookalikes: Golden-headed quetzal lives only in South America. Trogons in the same forests are smaller, with no streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Monteverde and San Gerardo de Dota (Costa Rica), and cloud forests of Guatemala's Verapaz
animal.season: Resident; easiest during breeding Mar–Jun, often near wild avocado (Lauraceae) trees

lore: Its feathers were reserved for Maya and Aztec nobility and priests, and the god Quetzalcoatl was the 'feathered serpent'. Guatemala's currency is the quetzal.
funFact: Legend says the quetzal's red breast was stained by the blood of the Kʼicheʼ hero Tecún Umán.

summary: A large red, yellow and blue parrot of tropical American forests. It gathers on riverbank clay licks in the Amazon to eat soil.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon basin
abilities: Beak cracks extremely hard nuts and seeds
Eats clay from riverbanks, possibly for sodium and to neutralise plant toxins
Flies at around 55 km/h
Can live for over 40 years and forms lifelong pair bonds

animal.diet: Seeds, nuts, fruit, flowers and nectar
animal.habitat: Humid lowland forest, especially near rivers
animal.behaviour: Pairs fly wingtip to wingtip and gather in noisy flocks at dawn at clay licks.
fieldMarks: Large scarlet parrot with a very long pointed tail
Yellow band across the upperwing, blue flight feathers
Bare white facial skin
Pale upper bill
animal.voice: Loud, harsh, far-carrying screeches, often given in flight
animal.lookalikes: Red-and-green macaw has green wing coverts instead of yellow and lines of tiny red feathers on its white face.
animal.whereToSee: Clay licks of Tambopata, Peru; Carara National Park and the Osa Peninsula, Costa Rica
animal.season: Resident

lore: Live scarlet macaws were traded north from Mexico to the ancestral Puebloans of Chaco Canyon around 900–1150 CE for their feathers. It is the national bird of Honduras.
funFact: Macaw skeletons at Pueblo Bonito suggest the birds were kept far from their native range a thousand years ago.

summary: The largest songbird, an all-black corvid with problem-solving skills that rival great apes. It lives across the Northern Hemisphere from deserts to the high Arctic.
nativeRange: Northern Hemisphere: North America, Europe, Asia and North Africa
abilities: Plans ahead and saves tools for later use (Kabadayi & Osvath 2017)
Caches food and re-hides it when watched by rivals
Mimics human speech and other sounds
Associates with wolves and human hunters to scavenge their kills
Plays, including sliding down snowy roofs

animal.diet: Omnivore: carrion, small animals, eggs, grain, refuse
animal.habitat: Almost any open or wooded habitat
animal.lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild; over 40 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Young ravens gather in winter roosts and share information about food sources.
fieldMarks: All-black, glossy, crow-like bird, much larger than crows
Heavy, deep bill
Shaggy throat feathers
Wedge-shaped tail in flight; often soars and tumbles
animal.voice: A deep, resonant croak 'prruk', plus a wide range of knocks and gurgles
animal.lookalikes: Carrion and American crows are smaller with thinner bills, square tails and cawing calls; they rarely soar.
animal.whereToSee: Mountain and coastal cliffs (e.g. Snowdonia, Wales); Yellowstone; a captive group at the Tower of London
animal.season: Resident

lore: Odin's ravens Huginn and Muninn ('thought' and 'memory') flew over the world bringing him news, and Raven is the trickster-creator who released the sun in Haida and Tlingit stories. Legend holds that Britain will fall if the Tower of London's ravens leave.
funFact: In Genesis, Noah sends out a raven before the dove.

summary: The largest and most widespread flamingo, gathering in tens of thousands on salt lakes and lagoons. Its pink comes from carotenoid pigments in the algae and crustaceans it eats.
nativeRange: Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Filter-feeds with its head upside down, pumping water through bill lamellae
Tolerates highly saline and alkaline lakes
Turns pink from dietary carotenoids such as canthaxanthin
Rubs pigment from preen-gland oil onto feathers as 'make-up' in breeding season
Both parents feed chicks a crop milk

animal.diet: Brine shrimp, small molluscs, insect larvae and algae
animal.habitat: Shallow saline and alkaline wetlands
animal.lifespan: Over 30 years in the wild; over 80 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Groups perform synchronised 'marching' displays, heads raised and turning, before breeding.
fieldMarks: Very tall, pale pink wading bird with long neck and legs
Pink bill with a black tip, bent sharply downward
Bright red and black wings in flight
Feeds with head upside down
animal.voice: Goose-like honking and grunting in flocks
animal.lookalikes: Lesser flamingo is smaller and deeper pink with a dark carmine bill that looks all-dark at a distance.
animal.whereToSee: Camargue (Pont de Gau), France; Rann of Kutch, India; Walvis Bay, Namibia
animal.season: Present all year at many wetlands; breeding colonies and numbers shift with water levels

lore: Pliny the Elder recorded that the Roman gourmet Apicius prized flamingo tongue as a delicacy. The Great Rann of Kutch in India hosts one of the largest breeding colonies, called 'Flamingo City'.
funFact: A captive greater flamingo at Adelaide Zoo lived to at least 83 years.

summary: A tall, grey bird of African swamps with a huge clog-shaped bill. It stands motionless for long periods before lunging to seize lungfish.
nativeRange: Swamps of East and Central Africa, from South Sudan to Zambia
abilities: Bill up to ~24 cm long and ~10 cm wide, with a sharp hooked tip
Stands still for very long periods to ambush prey
Collapses forward in a lunge to grab lungfish and catfish
Bill-clatters loudly as a greeting
Pours bills of water over eggs to cool them

animal.diet: Lungfish, catfish, tilapia, frogs, water snakes and young crocodiles
animal.habitat: Extensive papyrus and reed swamps
animal.behaviour: Usually two eggs hatch, but typically only one chick survives, the older outcompeting the younger.
fieldMarks: Very tall, grey stork-like bird
Huge, shoe-shaped bill with a hooked tip
Pale yellow eyes
Stands motionless for long periods
animal.voice: Mostly silent; adults clatter their bills at the nest
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable at close range; at a distance Goliath heron is slimmer with a long thin bill and rufous neck.
animal.whereToSee: Mabamba Swamp near Entebbe and Murchison Falls Delta (Uganda); Bangweulu Swamps (Zambia)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Ancient Egyptian art may depict shoebill-like birds. It was described scientifically in 1850 by John Gould from specimens from the White Nile.
funFact: Despite its stork-like look, its closest relatives are pelicans.

summary: A crested Amazonian bird that digests leaves by fermenting them in its crop, like a cow. Its chicks have claws on their wings and can climb back to the nest after escaping into water.
nativeRange: Amazon and Orinoco basins of South America
abilities: Foregut fermentation of leaves by bacteria in an enlarged crop
Chicks use two wing claws to climb branches
Chicks drop into water to escape predators and swim back
Smells strongly of manure from its fermenting crop
Sole living member of an ancient lineage

animal.diet: Leaves, buds and flowers of marsh plants
animal.habitat: Swamps, riverbanks and oxbow lakes
animal.behaviour: Groups nest communally in branches overhanging water, with helpers from previous broods aiding parents.
fieldMarks: Pheasant-sized bird with a spiky, ragged crest
Bare blue facial skin and red eyes
Brown above, buff breast, chestnut belly and wings
Clumsy flight over water
animal.voice: Hoarse hisses, grunts and wheezes
animal.lookalikes: No close lookalike; its odd shape and blue face are distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Oxbow lakes and rivers of the Amazon, e.g. Lake Sandoval (Tambopata, Peru) and Cuyabeno (Ecuador)
animal.season: Resident

lore: It is the national bird of Guyana. Its wing-clawed chicks were once compared to Archaeopteryx, though the claws evolved independently.
funFact: It is rarely hunted, because its meat is said to taste and smell foul.

summary: A long-billed shorebird holding the record for the longest nonstop flight of any bird. Godwits fly from Alaska to New Zealand and Australia across the Pacific without feeding, drinking or resting.
nativeRange: Breeds in Arctic Eurasia and Alaska; winters on coasts of Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Recorded nonstop flight of 13,560 km in about 11 days (Alaska to Tasmania, 2022)
Shrinks digestive organs before migration to carry more fat
Fat can make up over half its body weight at departure
Times departure to ride favourable winds from storm systems
Probes deep into mud for worms with a sensitive bill

animal.diet: Marine worms, molluscs and crustaceans; insects on breeding grounds
animal.habitat: Arctic tundra in summer; tidal mudflats in winter
animal.behaviour: Flocks leave Alaska in autumn on north winds and fly over the open Pacific for over a week.
fieldMarks: Large wader with a long, slightly upturned bill
Breeding male brick-red below
Winter birds grey-brown, streaked
Barred tail and no wing bar in flight
animal.voice: A nasal 'kirruk' or 'kew-kew'
animal.lookalikes: Black-tailed godwit has a straighter bill, longer legs, a bold white wing bar and a black tail band.
animal.whereToSee: Miranda (Firth of Thames) and Farewell Spit, New Zealand; the Wash and Morecambe Bay, England
animal.season: Breeds in the Arctic Jun–Jul; New Zealand Sep–Mar; Europe mainly in winter

lore: Māori knew kuaka as birds that flew to Hawaiki and beyond, and their departure marked seasons. Their epic flights were proven by satellite tags in 2007, when a female called E7 flew 11,680 km nonstop.
funFact: The record bird, tagged '234684', was only five months old when it made its flight.

summary: A cinnamon bird with a fan-shaped crest and zebra-striped wings, named for its soft 'oop-oop-oop' call. Nesting females and chicks defend themselves with a foul-smelling secretion produced with help from symbiotic bacteria.
nativeRange: Europe, Asia and Africa; European birds winter in sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Preen-gland secretion hosts Enterococcus bacteria that produce antimicrobials, protecting eggs
Nestlings squirt faeces and hiss like snakes at intruders
Probes soil with a long curved bill for larvae and mole crickets
Raises and fans its crest in alarm and on landing

animal.diet: Insects and larvae, especially beetle grubs and crickets; small reptiles
animal.habitat: Open ground with scattered trees, orchards and vineyards
animal.behaviour: Nests in tree holes or walls, where the female's oily secretion gives the nest a strong stench.
fieldMarks: Pinkish-cinnamon bird with a fan-shaped, black-tipped crest
Black and white barred wings and tail
Long, thin, down-curved bill
Floppy, butterfly-like flight
animal.voice: A soft, hollow 'oop-oop-oop'
animal.lookalikes: Distinctive; no similar bird in its range.
animal.whereToSee: Extremadura (Spain), the Algarve (Portugal) and orchards and villages across southern Europe and South Asia
animal.season: Europe: summer visitor Mar–Sep; resident in southern parts of its range

lore: In the Qur'an (Surah An-Naml) the hoopoe brings King Solomon news of the Queen of Sheba, and in Attar's 'Conference of the Birds' (12th c.) it leads the birds on their spiritual journey. It was named Israel's national bird in 2008.
funFact: Both Leviticus and Deuteronomy list the hoopoe among birds not to be eaten, yet it became Israel's national bird.

summary: A large pheasant of South Asia whose males raise and shiver a train of about 200 eye-spotted feathers. It is the national bird of India and has been carried as a royal ornament across the world for three thousand years.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Pakistan and Bangladesh; introduced widely
abilities: Train of elongated upper-tail coverts with iridescent structural-colour eyespots
Males rattle the train to produce low-frequency infrasound during displays
Kills and eats young cobras and other snakes
Loud alarm calls warn other animals of tigers and leopards

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, insects, small reptiles and snakes
animal.habitat: Forest edges, farmland and villages near water
animal.size: Males up to ~2.25 m including train; females ~1 m
animal.behaviour: Peahens choose mates partly on the vigour of the train-rattling display.
fieldMarks: Male: iridescent blue neck and breast, long green train with eyespots
Fan-shaped crest of spatula-tipped feathers
Female brown with a green neck and white belly
Large, often seen on the ground
animal.voice: A loud, wailing 'may-awe', often at dusk and before rain
animal.lookalikes: Green peafowl (Southeast Asia) has a green, scaly neck and a tufted upright crest.
animal.whereToSee: Ranthambore and Keoladeo (Bharatpur), India; Yala, Sri Lanka
animal.season: Resident; males display most during the pre-monsoon and monsoon breeding season and shed the train afterwards

lore: The peacock is Kartikeya's mount in Hindu tradition and Melek Taus, the Peacock Angel, in Yazidi faith; Mughal emperors sat on the Peacock Throne. Greeks said Hera set the hundred eyes of Argus on its tail.
funFact: Darwin wrote that 'the sight of a feather in a peacock's tail, whenever I gaze at it, makes me sick', because natural selection alone could not explain it.

summary: The most widespread swallow in the world, breeding across the Northern Hemisphere and wintering in the south. Its arrival has marked spring for farmers since antiquity.
nativeRange: Breeds across North America, Europe, North Africa and Asia; winters in South America, Africa, South Asia and Australasia
abilities: Migrates up to ~10,000 km, e.g. from Britain to South Africa
Catches insects in fast, low, agile flight
Builds cup nests from hundreds of mud pellets carried in its bill
Females prefer males with longer, more symmetrical tail streamers

animal.diet: Flying insects
animal.habitat: Open country near water, nesting in barns and under eaves
animal.behaviour: Pairs often return to the same barn each year, and earlier-brood young help feed later broods.
fieldMarks: Glossy steel-blue upperparts and breast band
Red forehead and throat
Long, deeply forked tail streamers
Swift, low, twisting flight
animal.voice: A cheerful twittering song with a grating trill; call a sharp 'vit'
animal.lookalikes: House martin has a white rump and short forked tail. Sand martin is brown. Red-rumped swallow has a pale rufous rump.
animal.whereToSee: Farmyards, stables and open country near water
animal.season: Europe and North America: summer visitor Apr–Sep

lore: Aristotle wrote that 'one swallow does not make a spring', and Gilbert White in the 18th century still wondered if swallows hibernated in mud. Sailors' swallow tattoos traditionally marked 5,000 nautical miles travelled.
funFact: It is the national bird of Austria and Estonia.

summary: A large white cockatoo of Australia and New Guinea with a bright yellow crest. In Sydney, cockatoos have learned to open wheelie-bin lids, a skill that spread from suburb to suburb through social learning.
nativeRange: Eastern and northern Australia, Tasmania, New Guinea and nearby islands; introduced to New Zealand
abilities: Learned bin-opening that spread socially, with local 'styles' (Klump et al. 2021)
A captive bird named Snowball (Cacatua galerita eleonora) dances in time to music, showing beat synchronisation
Flocks post sentinels that screech alarms
Can live 70 years or more in captivity

animal.diet: Seeds, roots, nuts, bulbs, berries and insect larvae
animal.habitat: Wooded country, farmland and city parks
animal.lifespan: 20–40 years in the wild; 70+ in captivity
animal.behaviour: Large, raucous flocks forage on the ground while some birds stand guard in trees.
fieldMarks: Large white cockatoo
Long, forward-curving yellow crest
Pale yellow wash under wings and tail
Dark grey bill
animal.voice: Very loud, harsh screeches
animal.lookalikes: Little corella and long-billed corella have no yellow crest and show bare bluish skin around the eye.
animal.whereToSee: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney and parks of eastern Australian cities
animal.season: Resident

lore: A cockatoo appears in a 13th-century manuscript of Emperor Frederick II's falconry treatise, having been gifted to him from the Sultan of Babylon, among the oldest European records of an Australasian bird.
funFact: Some Sydney cockatoos have also learned to turn on drinking-fountain taps.

summary: A glossy, speckled songbird whose winter flocks wheel at dusk in murmurations of hundreds of thousands. Introduced to North America in 1890, it now numbers in the tens of millions there.
nativeRange: Europe, Western Asia and North Africa; introduced to North America, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa
abilities: Murmurations: each bird tracks about seven neighbours, letting waves pass across the flock
Skilled mimic of other birds, phones and human speech
Navigates using a sun compass and magnetic sense
Opens its bill inside the soil to pry prey ('open-bill probing')

animal.diet: Insects, larvae, fruit and seeds
animal.habitat: Open fields, farmland, towns and cities
animal.lifespan: About 2–3 years on average; record over 22
animal.behaviour: Males decorate nests with aromatic green herbs, which may deter parasites.
fieldMarks: Short-tailed, glossy black bird with purple-green sheen
Pale-spotted in fresh winter plumage
Yellow bill in breeding season
Pointed, triangular wings in flight
animal.voice: Varied song of whistles, clicks, rattles and accurate mimicry
animal.lookalikes: Common blackbird has a longer tail, no gloss or spots, and hops rather than walks. Spotless starling (Iberia) is unspotted in summer.
animal.whereToSee: Winter murmurations at Brighton Palace Pier and RSPB Ham Wall (Somerset Levels), England
animal.season: Resident in much of Europe; murmurations Nov–Feb

lore: Mozart bought a pet starling in 1784 that could sing a theme from his Piano Concerto K.453, and buried it with a poem. Eugene Schieffelin released about 100 in New York's Central Park in 1890–91.
funFact: In Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 1, Hotspur plans to teach a starling to say 'Mortimer' to annoy the king.

summary: The wild ancestor of the domestic and city pigeon, probably the first bird tamed by humans. Homing pigeons can find their way back from hundreds of kilometres away, and carried messages for armies for millennia.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western and South Asia; feral populations worldwide
abilities: Homes over 1,000 km using sun compass, magnetic sense and landmarks
Possibly uses low-frequency infrasound for navigation
Both parents feed chicks 'crop milk'
Trained to tell paintings by Monet from Picasso (Watanabe et al. 1995)
Can recognise individual human faces

animal.diet: Seeds and grain; food scraps in cities
animal.habitat: Cliffs and ledges; buildings and bridges
animal.lifespan: 3–5 years in cities; up to 15+ in captivity
animal.behaviour: Pairs raise up to six broods a year, breeding in almost any season.
fieldMarks: Blue-grey pigeon with an iridescent green-purple neck
Two broad black bars on each wing
White rump (wild type)
Feral birds come in many colours
animal.voice: Soft, cooing 'oo-roo-coo'
animal.lookalikes: Stock dove has no white rump and only short black wing bars. Woodpigeon is larger with a white neck patch and white wing bands.
animal.whereToSee: Wild-type birds on sea cliffs of western Scotland and Ireland; feral flocks in almost every city
animal.season: Resident

lore: Pigeon posts relayed news for the Persians, Romans and Mughals, and a pigeon named Cher Ami saved nearly 200 American soldiers in 1918. Darwin bred fancy pigeons to illustrate artificial selection in 'On the Origin of Species'.
funFact: Reuters began in 1850 using pigeons to carry stock prices between Aachen and Brussels.

summary: A wild forest pheasant of South and Southeast Asia and the ancestor of the domestic chicken. With over 20 billion alive at any time, chickens are the most numerous bird on Earth.
nativeRange: Wild form from northern India to southern China and Indonesia; domestic chickens worldwide
abilities: Produces over a dozen distinct alarm and food calls, some referential (aerial vs ground predator)
Domestic hens can lay over 300 eggs a year
Roosters perform 'tidbitting', calling hens to food
Can run, roost in trees, and make short bursts of flight

animal.diet: Seeds, insects, fallen fruit and small animals
animal.habitat: Forest edges, scrub and clearings
animal.behaviour: A rooster gives different alarm calls for hawks overhead and for ground predators, and hens respond appropriately.
fieldMarks: Male: orange-gold hackles, red comb and wattles, long dark green arching tail
Female brown with a small comb
Wild males have slate-grey legs
Wild males moult into a dull eclipse plumage after breeding
