animal.voice: Crow is like a domestic rooster's but shorter, ending abruptly
animal.lookalikes: Feral and domestic chickens interbreed with it; mixed birds often have yellow or pale legs and lack the eclipse moult. Grey junglefowl of peninsular India has grey, spotted hackles.
animal.whereToSee: Jim Corbett National Park (India), Khao Yai and Kaeng Krachan (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Domesticated in Southeast Asia around 3,500 years ago, chickens were first kept for cockfighting and ritual before food. Roman generals consulted sacred chickens before battle, and Socrates' last words asked that a rooster be offered to Asclepius.
funFact: Most of the world's influenza vaccines are still grown in fertilised chicken eggs.

summary: An Australian bird whose males build a two-walled stick avenue and decorate it with blue objects to court females. The female chooses a mate by inspecting his bower and display.
nativeRange: Eastern and south-eastern Australia
abilities: Builds an avenue bower of hundreds of sticks
Collects blue items such as feathers, flowers, bottle caps and straws
Paints the bower walls with chewed plant juice, sometimes using a wad of bark as a tool
Mimics other birds' calls during display

animal.diet: Fruit, leaves and insects
animal.habitat: Moist forest and adjacent woodland and gardens
animal.behaviour: Males take seven years to gain their glossy blue-black plumage, and young males build practice bowers while still green.
fieldMarks: Adult male glossy blue-black with violet-blue eyes
Female and young males olive-green with scalloped underparts
Pale yellowish bill
Males build an avenue bower of sticks decorated with blue objects
animal.voice: Loud whistles, buzzing and mechanical sounds, and mimicry at the bower
animal.lookalikes: Young males look like females for several years. Regent bowerbird male is black and gold.
animal.whereToSee: Lamington National Park (O'Reilly's), Queensland; Blue Mountains, NSW; Canberra's Australian National Botanic Gardens
animal.season: Resident; bowers most active in spring and early summer

lore: Nineteenth-century naturalists such as John Gould puzzled over bowers as 'playing-places', and Darwin discussed them in 'The Descent of Man' (1871) as evidence of aesthetic choice in sexual selection.
funFact: Males steal blue decorations from rivals' bowers and sometimes wreck them.

summary: The national bird of Papua New Guinea, shown on its flag. Males gather at forest leks, clapping their wings and shaking their heads as they raise cascades of orange-red flank plumes to court females.
nativeRange: Southern and north-eastern New Guinea
abilities: Males display communally at leks, raising and shaking plumes
Raises plumes into an erect fan while calling loudly
Disperses seeds of many rainforest trees
Hybridises with other Paradisaea species where ranges meet

animal.diet: Fruit, especially figs; also arthropods
animal.habitat: Rainforest and forest edge
animal.size: About 34 cm, plus male tail wires
animal.behaviour: A dozen or more males display in the same tree, and females visit to choose among them.
fieldMarks: Male: maroon-brown body, yellow crown and collar, dark emerald throat
Long red to orange flank plumes
Two long black tail wires
Female drab maroon-brown with no plumes or wires
animal.lookalikes: Lesser bird-of-paradise has yellow plumes; the two hybridise where they meet. Plume colour varies among Raggiana subspecies from deep red to apricot.
animal.whereToSee: Varirata National Park near Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea
animal.season: Resident; display at morning leks

lore: Plumes have been worn for centuries in New Guinea headdresses, and traded to Asia; in the 16th century legless skins reached Europe, giving rise to the myth that birds-of-paradise never landed. PNG adopted it as its flag emblem in 1971.
funFact: Named after Francesco Raggi, an Italian marquis from Genoa.

summary: A huge hornbill of South and Southeast Asian forests, with a yellow casque atop its bill. During nesting, the female seals herself inside a tree cavity and depends on the male to feed her through a slit.
nativeRange: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Southeast Asia to Sumatra
abilities: Female walls herself into the nest with mud and droppings for months
Male delivers fruit regurgitated one at a time through the slit
Major disperser of large-seeded rainforest trees, especially figs
Its loud wingbeats can be heard from far away

animal.diet: Mainly figs and other fruit; also small animals
animal.habitat: Tall old-growth forest
animal.lifespan: Up to about 50 years in captivity
animal.behaviour: Birds rub preen-gland secretions onto the casque and wings, giving them their yellow colour.
fieldMarks: Very large black-and-white hornbill
Huge yellow bill with a broad, concave casque
White tail with a black band
Loud whooshing wingbeats
animal.voice: Pairs duet with a rapid mix of loud roars and barks, starting from a steady 'kok'
animal.lookalikes: Rhinoceros hornbill (Sunda region) has an upturned red-and-orange casque. Wreathed hornbill has no casque and a white tail without a band.
animal.whereToSee: Pakke Tiger Reserve (Arunachal Pradesh) and Valparai in the Anamalai Hills, India; Khao Yai, Thailand
animal.season: Resident; breeds Jan–Apr, when pairs are most vocal

lore: It is the state bird of Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh, and Naga peoples traditionally used its feathers and casques in headdresses; Nagaland's Hornbill Festival is named for it.
funFact: Its casque is mostly hollow and light, unlike the solid ivory-like casque of its relative the helmeted hornbill.

summary: A huge, pale-brown vulture that soars on thermals over mountains, finding carcasses by watching other vultures. Colonies clean up dead livestock and wildlife, reducing disease.
nativeRange: Southern Europe, North Africa, Middle East and Central Asia to India
abilities: Soars for hours on thermals with barely a wingbeat
A group can strip a carcass in under an hour
Extremely acidic stomach kills many pathogens in rotting meat
Spots feeding vultures from kilometres away and follows them

animal.diet: Carrion of large mammals
animal.habitat: Open mountainous country with cliffs for nesting
animal.behaviour: Nests in cliff colonies, laying a single egg each year.
fieldMarks: Huge vulture with pale sandy-brown body
White fluffy neck ruff and pale head
Dark flight feathers contrasting with paler wing coverts
Soars on long, broad, 'fingered' wings
animal.voice: Hisses, grunts and cackles at carcasses
animal.lookalikes: Cinereous vulture is darker all over. Rüppell's vulture (Africa) has scaly, pale-edged feathers. Egyptian vulture is smaller and white with black flight feathers.
animal.whereToSee: Monfragüe National Park (Spain), Gorges du Verdon (France), and the Strait of Gibraltar on migration
animal.season: Resident; young birds cross the Strait of Gibraltar in autumn

lore: The 'eagle' (nesher) of the Hebrew Bible is likely the griffon vulture, and Tibetan and Zoroastrian sky burials relied on vultures. It was reintroduced to France's Grands Causses in the 1980s.
funFact: The veterinary drug diclofenac, deadly to Gyps vultures, wiped out over 95% of India's related vultures in the 1990s.

summary: A large white swan with an orange bill and a black knob. One of the heaviest flying birds, it is less vocal than other swans but hisses fiercely in defence.
nativeRange: Europe and Asia; introduced in North America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Among the heaviest flying birds, up to about 15 kg
Wingbeats make a loud throbbing sound audible far away
Upends to graze aquatic plants up to a metre deep
Defends nest aggressively with wing displays ('busking')

animal.diet: Aquatic plants; some invertebrates
animal.habitat: Lakes, rivers, estuaries and park ponds
animal.behaviour: Pairs often stay together for many years, and cygnets ride on their parents' backs.
fieldMarks: Very large white swan
Orange bill with a black knob at the base
Neck held in an S-curve
Wings often raised in an arch when threatened
animal.voice: Mostly quiet; hisses and snorts; wings make a loud throbbing sound in flight
animal.lookalikes: Whooper swan has a yellow-and-black bill and straight neck. Trumpeter and tundra swans in North America have black bills.
animal.whereToSee: Abbotsbury Swannery, Dorset; park lakes and rivers across Europe
animal.season: Resident; cygnets May–Jun

lore: The British monarch claims ownership of unmarked mute swans in open water, and an annual 'Swan Upping' on the Thames counts them. Zeus approached Leda as a swan in Greek myth.
funFact: The 'swan song' legend, that it sings only at death, dates back to the ancient Greeks.

summary: One of the rarest cranes, famous for its paired courtship dances in the snow. It symbolises longevity and fidelity in East Asia.
nativeRange: Breeds in south-east Russia and north-east China; winters in Korea and eastern China; resident in Hokkaido, Japan
abilities: Pairs perform synchronised duets and leaping dances
Migrates between Siberian marshes and Korean and Chinese wetlands
Hokkaido population is non-migratory
Can live 30+ years

animal.diet: Fish, crabs, insects, amphibians and rice
animal.habitat: Wetlands with tall reeds and shallow water
animal.size: ~1.5 m tall; wingspan up to 2.5 m
animal.behaviour: Couples bond for life and greet each other with bowing, leaping and loud unison calls.
fieldMarks: Tall white crane with a red crown patch
Black neck and face
Black secondary flight feathers, looking like a black tail when standing
Pure white primary feathers
animal.voice: Loud, trumpeting unison calls given by pairs
animal.lookalikes: Siberian crane has a red face and black primaries. White-naped crane is grey-bodied.
animal.whereToSee: Tsurui-Ito Tancho Crane Sanctuary and Akan International Crane Center, Hokkaido; Zhalong Nature Reserve, China
animal.season: Hokkaido cranes are resident, with winter feeding gatherings Nov–Mar

lore: In Japan folding 1,000 paper cranes (senbazuru) grants a wish, made famous by Sadako Sasaki after Hiroshima; it appears on Japan Airlines' logo. In China it is linked with immortals and longevity.
funFact: Hokkaido's population fell to about 20 birds in the 1920s; winter feeding by local farmers helped it recover to over 1,800.
